title: The Zeigarnik Effect Is Running Your Life https://www.thebestleadershipnewsletter.com/p/zeigarnik-effect-youre-not-busy-you-have-open-loops
author: The Best Leadership Newsletter
summary: This article introduces the Zeigarnik Effect -- Bluma Zeigarnik's 1920s discovery that incomplete tasks are retained in memory far more persistently than completed ones -- as an explanatory framework for why leaders with many unfinished responsibilities cannot stop thinking about work, even when nominally off the clock. The brain's drive for closure keeps open loops active in working memory, draining cognitive resources around the clock. The author applies this to leadership specifically: leaders do not just carry their own open loops but inadvertently create them in others by making ambiguous requests, leaving decisions pending, or opening conversations that don't reach resolution. The article argues that the solution is not willpower or work-life balance programs but systematic loop closure: clear commitments, completed decisions, and explicit acknowledgment of what is and is not being pursued. The piece ends with practical diagnostics drawn from executive coaching about the categories of leadership behavior that generate the most inadvertent open loops.
points: The Zeigarnik Effect -- proven in 1920s experiments where subjects recalled interrupted tasks far better than completed ones -- explains why leaders who seem to 'have balance' still cannot stop thinking about work: incomplete tasks persist in memory until resolved.

Leaders don't just carry their own open loops; they generate them in others through ambiguous asks, deferred decisions, and conversations that end without resolution -- multiplying the cognitive load across the team.

The wakefulness pattern many leaders attribute to dedication or passion is neurological, not motivational: the brain literally will not release unresolved tasks, making chronic mental overwork a biology problem rather than a character problem.

Systematic loop closure -- not work-life balance rhetoric or motivational reframing -- is the practical solution: clear commits, explicit decision points, and deliberate acknowledgment of what is not being pursued all release the brain from its holding pattern.

Executive coaching diagnostics reveal that the most loop-generating leader behaviors cluster around ambiguity: leaders who ask without specifying, decide without communicating, or initiate without completing create disproportionate cognitive drag in their organizations.

So like any good, over-achieving Russian psychologist in the 1920s, she ran some experiments to test this phenomenon. She gave people a series of tasks and let them finish some, while forcing others to be left unfinished.
However, if I were a guessing man - which I am - I'd guess that you're probably like me. You don't have one unfinished thing on your mind, you have 47 of them.

In fact, here are ways you're probably creating open loops and not even recognizing it: When you tell yourself you should delegate more [ ] - that's an open loop. When you hand off a project but say "keep me updated" - that loop stays open.

Maybe you tell yourself that you're great at compartmentalizing and you're just going to let these unfinished things go. If you're like me, you think you're being a good leader or an exceptional worker [ ] by staying on top of all the things you need to do.
You shove one more incomplete idea into any open spot and tell yourself it'll be fine. They add up to a heck of a lot of mental weight to carry around.

In fact, while we're focused on closing loops, you should probably change your daily To-Do List habit too. It's better to finish 4 of 4 tasks in a day and feel complete, than it is to finish 4 of 9 and feel like the day just got away from you.
